title: Paper trading platform I've been grinding on for months. PowerShell, 79 scripts, A/B test between two books, code enforced bear halt. Sharing the stack and the lessons.
author: Cold-Fix-884
selftext:
Built this over the last few months. Sharing the engineering, not the strategy. There's no strategy worth talking about, it's all in the controls.



Stack is PowerShell. I know. It started as one script that emailed me a premarket digest and somewhere along the way it became 79 scripts and about 26k lines, with a dashboard webapp that serves on localhost:8765. The main dashboard file alone is 10,277 lines. State is JSON, all writes go through a temp+rename helper because I corrupted a trades.json once writing during a crash and that was enough.



The setup. Three paper trading books running off Alpaca's sandbox API. Stocks (split into A and B for an A/B test), options swing, and crypto. There's also a manual book tracker for discretionary entries that aren't from the automated trader. Universe is about 289 tickers. The stocks scanner scores setups from a combined feed: technicals (SMA200/50, ATR, RSI, IV Rank), insider transactions, earnings windows, short squeeze signals (with feeds for fails to deliver, WSB sentiment, broader social, and the SVR short volume ratio), macro indicators, and a sector rotation read. The options swing path adds an IV aware contract sizer. The crypto trader pulls funding rates, the fear and greed index, mean reversion bands, and a crypto specific macro signal layer, then runs at a tighter loop. Crypto's currently paused. I have about a week of forward data still to collect before adding more features. That's a discipline thing.



The A/B test is the honest part. Book A only trades the top 5 scored setups per scan. Book B trades the full \~89 name pool. Both books gate identically on the same regime halt so they can't desync on a macro call. If the scorer has edge over a random draw from the eligible pool, A should beat B over enough trades. If it doesn't, you find out. I was running them for weeks before I caught a bug where Book A was starving on duplicate ticker skips while Book B kept trading. That made the comparison unfair by construction. Fixed. The edge analyzer that compares them does stratified matched N with a Welch t test and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. There's a random baseline backtester for the same reason. "Did the scorer beat random?" is the actual question. The shares analyzer does it right. The options random baseline is still on my open issue list (unmatched N, no t test). I'll get to it.



The controls layer is where the work went. I stress tested the shares strategy through April to December 2022 to see what it would have done in a real bear. Win rate dropped from 53.4% (bull) to 35.7%. Break even on the r/R is 40%. So it's documented as bull only, and the trader now blocks new entries when SPY closes below the 50 DMA for 5 consecutive trading days. Code enforced, not just a banner. I tested a per signal 200 DMA gate on five separate windows before deciding on this. It helped one window, hurt two, neutral two. So I rejected the per signal version and kept only the coarse book level halt. There's also a 12% equity drawdown circuit breaker, an earnings blackout window of ±3 trading days, a correlation cap that blocks adding a position too correlated to existing positions, a sector concentration cap, a daily new entry cap, a cash reservation rule, and a slippage model in basis points. Each one of these added one or two skip reasons to the daily log. Looking at the trade log and seeing entries like NVDA blocked because correlation to AMD is 0.83 against the 0.70 cap makes the system feel like it's actually guarding something.



Every signal carries a thesis string. No thesis, no entry. The point isn't to be clever. It's to give you context six weeks later when you're staring at a closed trade and trying to remember why you took it. The setup journal logs every signal that ever fired with its thesis, the score components, the regime at the time, the resulting fill, and the eventual outcome. There's a separate decision log for every config change, every manual override, every halt I manually invoked. There's an override audit CSV that flags any time the manual book disagreed with the systematic book. Tracking those disagreements is the only honest way to know whether discretionary discipline is helping or hurting.



The research arm runs separately from the live books. Backtest harness, out of sample split tool, pattern experiment runner, vol experiment runner, crypto specific backtester. A coin relative strength tester. A share edge analyzer. Performance attribution by setup type. Tax analysis. A track record reporter. Journal analytics that break down win rate by sector, by setup type, by IV Rank bucket. Trade analytics that compute per trade slippage in bps so I can see if the assumed slippage in the backtester is realistic. None of this is novel and most of it took longer than I expected.



The ops layer is what makes it usable. Premarket digest email lands in my inbox before open every day. Setups, regime status, open positions, drawdown warnings, sector concentration, anything blacked out for earnings. Crypto digest is separate. Setup alerts fire intraday if a high conviction setup forms. Experiment alerts fire if a backtest produces a result that meets the promotion threshold. An offsite backup runs nightly. Equity verification runs against the broker every morning. Price source verification cross checks a second vendor (technically still both Yahoo right now. That's on my open list to fix, it doesn't actually meet the two source spec). There's a data quality auditor and a staleness checker that surface warnings in the digest. Everything runs as Windows scheduled tasks except the main dashboard webserver which runs as a long lived background process.



The governance layer is where most "trading bot" projects don't have anything. Written Investment Policy Statement that defines what counts as a tradeable setup, what triggers a halt, what the position size ladder is, and what the bear regime rule is. A kill list of strategies that ran for long enough to fail validation and got formally retired. A hypotheses log of what's currently being tested and what threshold a hypothesis has to clear to get promoted into the live scorer. An incident log with postmortems for every meaningful failure. The 118 hour outage from a child process crash with no stderr redirect is in there, with the fix and the followup items. An external audit document I wrote against myself with P0/P1/P2 severity classified findings and a remediation tracker. The audit currently has six P0 findings open. That's normal. The honest version of any system has more open bugs than closed ones.



Things I haven't solved. Entry fills against a 6 hour old cached spot price. Top of the open P0 list, biases every fill and stop anchor. Options multi contract P&L is understated everywhere because the suggestedContracts field never gets persisted into the journal. Default backtest range is 1y which collapses the SMA200 warmup window into about 47 usable bars. Random baseline for options isn't matched N stratified. Cross source price verification is illusory (both sources are currently Yahoo). The 12% drawdown breaker was dead two ways before this week's audit and is now fixed, but the realized drawdown calc still treats open positions at entry cost so it's blind to unrealized DD. None of this is hidden. It's all in the audit doc with severity classifications and fix in progress markers.



The lesson I keep relearning: the strategy doesn't matter that much. The controls do. Treating "decision correctness" as the product instead of "PnL" was the unlock, because in a paper context PnL is fake but bad decisions are real and they teach you the wrong lessons for when you go live.



Happy to answer questions on the engineering. Don't ask me what the strategy is. There isn't one worth telling.
